claims.claim: Of all the NMD factors tested (UPF1115-914, UPF2, UPF3b, EJC, and DHX34), only DHX34 interacted directly with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 forming a stable complex.
claims.source: We first tested the interaction between RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes and UPF1115-914 (a truncated version lacking the flexible N- and C-terminal ends of UPF1), UPF2, UPF3b, EJC, and DHX34 by pull-down experiments using the His-tag in RUVBL1 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D). Of all these, only DHX34 interacted directly with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 forming a stable complex that has not been previously described.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: When DHX34 was pulled down from cells, both RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 were detected by western blot.
claims.source: We then verified the in vitro results using immunoprecipitation experiments from cells. When DHX34 was pulled down from cells, both RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 were detected by western blot (Figure 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: FLAG-RUVBL1 eluted also endogenous RUVBL1 and RUVBL2, in agreement with the oligomeric nature of the complexes formed by these ATPases.
claims.source: FLAG-RUVBL1 eluted also endogenous RUVBL1 and RUVBL2, in agreement with the oligomeric nature of the complexes formed by these ATPases.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation that supports the oligomeric nature of the complex.

claims.claim: SMG1 forms a direct complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
claims.source: A pull-down experiment using the His-tag in RUVBL1 revealed that SMG1 forms a direct complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 and similar results were obtained in pull-down experiments using a FLAG-tag in SMG1 as bait.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pull-down experiments.

claims.claim: The formation of a complex between RUVBL1-RUVBL2 and SMG1 excludes SMG8 and SMG9.
claims.source: Curiously, in both types of experiments, SMG1 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2 interact but SMG8 and SMG9 were undetected in the elution, suggesting that the formation of a complex between RUVBL1-RUVBL2 and SMG1 exclude SMG8 and SMG9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: 2D averages of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 revealed hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes with putative density for DHX34 located at the DII-face of the ring.
claims.source: 2D averages of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 revealed hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes with putative density for DHX34 located at the DII-face of the ring.
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM image analysis.

claims.claim: The interaction of DHX34 disrupts the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 dodecameric double-ring complexes.
claims.source: The interaction of DHX34 disrupts the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 dodecameric double-ring complexes, an effect observed before in the assembly of R2TP (Martino et al., 2018; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: DHX34 attaches to the DII-face of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring flexibly.
claims.source: An extensive 2D and 3D classification strategy of the images revealed that DHX34 attaches to the DII-face of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring flexibly and we selected the most homogenous sub-group of particles for refinement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM image processing and classification.

claims.claim: The structure of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 was determined at an average resolution of 5.0 Å.
claims.source: The structure of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 was determined at an average resolution of 5.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), with local resolutions up to 4.1 Å for the core RUVBL1-RUVBL2 whereas the resolution of DHX34 in the complex was around 8–10 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B — Figure 2—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claims.claim: The local resolution for the core RUVBL1-RUVBL2 was up to 4.1 Å whereas the resolution of DHX34 in the complex was around 8–10 Å.
claims.source: The structure of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 was determined at an average resolution of 5.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), with local resolutions up to 4.1 Å for the core RUVBL1-RUVBL2 whereas the resolution of DHX34 in the complex was around 8–10 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B — Figure 2—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM structure determination showing differential resolution.

claims.claim: The disparity in resolution between DHX34 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2 in the complex was a strong indication of the flexible attachment of DHX34 to the ATPases.
claims.source: The disparity in resolution between DHX34 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2 in the complex was a strong indication of the flexible attachment of DHX34 to the ATPases.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the resolution differences observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: DHX34 binds to the internal regions of the DII domains in the hetero-hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring.
claims.source: DHX34 binds to the internal regions of the DII domains in the hetero-hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring.
claims.evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: The DII external domains (OB-folds) are mostly free and potentially accessible for interaction with other partners.
claims.source: The DII external domains (OB-folds) are mostly free and potentially accessible for interaction with other partners (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure with speculation about functional implications.

claims.claim: DHX34 contacts several RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 subunits of the complex, thus inducing global conformational changes in the structure of the ATPases.
claims.source: DHX34 contacts several RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 subunits of the complex, thus inducing global conformational changes in the structure of the ATPases (see below).
claims.evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure analysis.

claims.claim: The average resolution of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 improved to 4.2 Å when using a mask that removed the influence of DHX34 and the protruding OB-fold domains during image processing.
claims.source: We first analyzed the structure of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring using a mask that removed the influence of DHX34 and the protruding OB-fold domains during image processing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This way the average resolution of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 improved to 4.2 Å (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, Table 1) detecting the presence or absence of nucleotide in the nucleotide-binding pockets of both subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM image processing.

claims.claim: The most striking feature in the cryo-EM map is that the N-terminal regions that contribute to nucleotide binding are visualized in RUVBL1 but not in any of the three RUVBL2 subunits.
claims.source: The most striking feature in the cryo-EM map is that the N-terminal regions that contribute to nucleotide binding (Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019; Silva et al., 2018) are visualized in RUVBL1 but not in any of the three RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a key observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: DHX34 induces changes that affect the conformation of RUVBL2 N-terminal regions in all three subunits of the complex.
claims.source: Based on these observations, we conclude that DHX34 induce changes that affect the conformation of RUVBL2 N-terminal regions in all three subunits of the complex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on extensive cryo-EM classification experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 3-5.

claims.claim: The conformational changes in the N-terminus of RUVBL2 were coupled to the loss of nucleotide.
claims.source: The conformational changes in the N-terminus of RUVBL2 were coupled to the loss of nucleotide (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: RUVBL1-RUVBL2 co-purifies with nucleotides bound to all six subunits.
claims.source: We and others have observed that RUVBL1-RUVBL2 co-purifies with nucleotides bound to all six subunits (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019), but whereas nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1 in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex (Figure 3D), this is lost in all three RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous observations and the current cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: Nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1 in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex.
claims.source: We and others have observed that RUVBL1-RUVBL2 co-purifies with nucleotides bound to all six subunits (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019), but whereas nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1 in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex (Figure 3D), this is lost in all three RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: Nucleotide is lost in all three RUVBL2 subunits in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex.
claims.source: We and others have observed that RUVBL1-RUVBL2 co-purifies with nucleotides bound to all six subunits (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019), but whereas nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1 in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex (Figure 3D), this is lost in all three RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: The absence of density for nucleotide in RUVBL2 could not be attributed to a lack of sufficient resolution because nucleotides are clearly present in all RUVBL1 subunits in the same complex at similar resolution.
claims.source: The absence of density for nucleotide in RUVBL2 could not be attributed to a lack of sufficient resolution because nucleotides are clearly present in all RUVBL1 subunits in the same complex at similar resolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is an argument based on comparing the resolution in different parts of the structure.

claims.claim: DHX34 induces conformational changes in other regions of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 besides the N-termini of RUVBL2.
claims.source: DHX34 induces conformational changes in other regions of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 besides the N-termini of RUVBL2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B — Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in the figures and video.

claims.claim: These changes affect mostly to the internal regions of the DII domains and regions in the AAA-ring.
claims.source: These changes affect mostly to the internal regions of the DII domains and regions in the AAA-ring.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: These changes do not affect key residues of the RUVBL1 nucleotide-binding pocket, which explains why ADP remains bound to RUVBL1 after the interaction with DHX34.
claims.source: These changes do not affect key residues of the RUVBL1 nucleotide-binding pocket, which explains why ADP remains bound to RUVBL1 after the interaction with DHX34 (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The structure of the nucleotide-binding pocket in RUVBL2 is not altered significantly with respect to the crystal structure of RUVBL2 bound to nucleotide.
claims.source: The structure of the nucleotide-binding pocket in RUVBL2 is not altered significantly with respect to the crystal structure of RUVBL2 bound to nucleotide (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: It is the displacement of the N-termini of RUVBL2 that is mostly responsible for the loss of nucleotide.
claims.source: This suggests that it is the displacement of the N-termini of RUVBL2 that is mostly responsible for the loss of nucleotide.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural observations.

claims.claim: DHX34 affects nucleotide binding of every RUVBL2 subunit in the complex by stabilizing a conformation that displaces the N-termini of RUVBL2.
claims.source: Together, our results reveal that DHX34 affects nucleotide binding of every RUVBL2 subunit in the complex by stabilizing a conformation that displaces the N-termini of RUVBL2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data.

claims.claim: The dimensions of the DHX34 density that we observe attached to one ring of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 can only agree with one copy of DHX34.
claims.source: This comparison revealed that the dimensions of the DHX34 density that we observe attached to one ring of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 can only agree with one copy of DHX34, and that possibly, it is the DHX34 core domains and not the CTD that interact with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of cryo-EM volumes.

claims.claim: Purified DHX34 can still bind RUVBL1-RUVBL2 when its flexible C-terminal domain has been deleted.
claims.source: Accordingly, purified DHX34 can still bind RUVBL1-RUVBL2 when its flexible C-terminal domain has been deleted (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The approximate mass of the volume occupied by DHX34 in the complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 is around 120 kDa.
claims.source: In addition, we estimated that the approximate mass of the volume occupied by DHX34 in the complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 is around 120 kDa by using the volume programme in EMAN (Ludtke et al., 1999) (https://blake.bcm.edu/emanwiki/Volume).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational mass estimation from the cryo-EM volume.

claims.claim: Monomeric DHX34 and the DHX34 core domains alone have a molecular mass of 132 kDa and 111 kDa, respectively.
claims.source: Monomeric DHX34 and the DHX34 core domains alone have a molecular mass of 132 kDa and 111 kDa, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is based on calculation from the protein sequence.

claims.claim: One copy DHX34 interacts with one RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hexamer forming a complex with 3:3:1 stoichiometry.
claims.source: Together, these analyses strongly suggest that one copy DHX34 interacts with one RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hexamer forming a complex with 3:3:1 stoichiometry.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including volume analysis and deletion experiments.

claims.claim: All single domain deletions of DHX34 retained binding to RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 to a measurable degree.
claims.source: We first tested a series of systematic domain deletion mutants and found that all single domain deletions retained binding to RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 to a measurable degree (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: No domain of DHX34 is sufficient and necessary on its own to mediate the interaction with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
claims.source: As shown by the quantification in Figure 4D, no domain is sufficient and necessary on its own to mediate the interaction with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the domain deletion experiments.

claims.claim: Heavily N- and C- terminal truncated versions of DHX34 showed a pronounced reduction in binding to RUVBL1-RUVBL2 but they could still bind to the ATPases.
claims.source: Heavily N- and C- terminal truncated versions of DHX34 showed a pronounced reduction in binding to RUVBL1-RUVBL2 but they could still bind to the ATPases (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Several interactions through different domains are made between DHX34 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
claims.source: Overall this analysis indicated that several interactions through different domains are made between DHX34 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2, which agrees with the structure of the complex that shows multiple regions of contact between DHX34 and the ATPases.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the domain deletion experiments and structural data.

claims.claim: His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2E300Q forms similar oligomers to the wild-type complex.
claims.source: We found that His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2E300Q forms similar oligomers to the wild-type complex and, in addition, it behaves similarly to His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 when their intrinsic fluorescence was measured using a thermal denaturation assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and thermal stability data.

claims.claim: DHX34D279A showed an ATP consumption of 24.2% compared with wild-type DHX34.
claims.source: DHX34D279A showed an ATP consumption of 24.2% compared with wild-type (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: DHX34 is not affected by 20 min incubation time at 37°C but it is affected by 40 min.
claims.source: We found that DHX34 is not affected by 20 min incubation time but it is by 40 min when compared to freshly purified DHX34 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is based on thermal stability measurements.

claims.claim: The weak ATPase activity of His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 measured at 37°C (4.9 ± 0.8 min−1 of ATP turnover) is similar to what had been determined previously by others.
claims.source: The weak ATPase activity of His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 that we measured at 37°C (4.9 ± 0.8 min−1 of ATP turnover) is similar to what had been determined previously by others (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and this value was set as 100% activity for comparison with subsequent measurements (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is based on ATPase activity measurements and comparison with previous studies.

claims.claim: His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q and His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 complexes showed a significant reduction of their ATPase activity (43% and 20% ATPase activity respectively, compared to wild-type His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2).
claims.source: His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q and His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 complexes that are mutants in only one of the two subunits showed a significant reduction of their ATPase activity as expected if not all the subunits in each oligomer are active (43% and 20% ATPase activity for His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q and His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2, respectively, compared to wild-type His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: Adding DHX34 to His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 reduced the ATPase activity around 50% (2.5 ± 0.9 min−1).
claims.source: Interestingly, the ATPase activity was reduced around 50% (2.5 ± 0.9 min−1) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a key finding supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: Adding DHX34 caused no effects in His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q complexes containing ATPase-dead RUVBL2 subunits.
claims.source: Most interestingly, adding DHX34 caused no effects in His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q complexes containing ATPase-dead RUVBL2 subunits (His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q showed rates of 2.1 ± 0.5 and 2.0 ± 0.5 min−1 in the absence and presence of DHX34D279A, respectively) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a key finding supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: ATP hydrolysis by the His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 mutant was affected by DHX34 as in the wild-type.
claims.source: In contrast, ATP hydrolysis by the His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 mutant was affected by DHX34 as in the wild-type (His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 showed rates of 1.0 ± 0.3 and 0.4 ± 0.1 min−1 in the absence and presence of DHX34D279A, respectively) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a key finding supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: DHX34 actions on the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex are mediated mostly by changes in the RUVBL2 subunits.
claims.source: These results are fully in agreement with a model where DHX34 actions on the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex are mediated mostly by changes in the RUVBL2 subunits.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ATPase activity measurements with different mutants.

claims.claim: Removal of the His-tag from RUVBL1 had a small effect on the rate of ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex (3.6 ± 0.7 min-).
claims.source: Removal of the tag had a small effect on the rate of ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex (3.6 ± 0.7 min-) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B) but addition of DHX34 caused a similar reduction of ATP hydrolysis (1.0 ± 0.5 min−1), indicating that the presence of the tag does not interfere with the action of DHX34 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: Addition of DHX34 to untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2 caused a similar reduction of ATP hydrolysis (1.0 ± 0.5 min−1), indicating that the presence of the tag does not interfere with the action of DHX34.
claims.source: Removal of the tag had a small effect on the rate of ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex (3.6 ± 0.7 min-) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B) but addition of DHX34 caused a similar reduction of ATP hydrolysis (1.0 ± 0.5 min−1), indicating that the presence of the tag does not interfere with the action of DHX34 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: DHX34 caused a reduction in the ATPase activity of untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes when RUVBL1 was mutated but not when RUVBL2 was mutated.
claims.source: As in the case of complexes containing His-RUVBL1, DHX34 caused a reduction in the ATPase activity of untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes when RUVBL1 was mutated but not when RUVBL2 was mutated (Untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q mutant consumed 2.0 ± 0.5 and 1.8 ± 0.1 min−1 in the absence and presence of DHX34D279A, respectively; and untagged RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 mutant showed rates of 1.1 ± 0.5 and 0.5 ± 0.2 min−1 in the absence and presence of DHX34D279A, respectively) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: There is a correlation between the conformational changes induced by DHX34 and the ATP hydrolysis activity of the complex.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that there is a correlation between the conformational changes induced by DHX34 and the ATP hydrolysis activity of the complex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined structural and biochemical data.

claims.claim: DHX34 regulates ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex mostly by changes in the RUVBL2 subunit.
claims.source: Thus, DHX34 regulates ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex mostly by changes in the RUVBL2 subunit.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ATPase activity measurements with different mutants.

claims.claim: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 directly interact with a subset of factors involved in the initiation of the NMD response.
claims.source: Several lines of evidence show that the ATPase activity of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 regulates several cellular processes. In particular, RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 ATPase activity is needed for a fully functional NMD response and for normal levels of SMG1-mediated UPF1 phosphorylation in vivo (Izumi et al., 2010; however, how these ATPases regulate NMD was completely unknown. Here, we provide evidence that RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 directly interact with a subset of factors involved in the initiation of the NMD response and these interactions can affect greatly the conformation of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 oligomers and their ATPase activity.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: These interactions can affect greatly the conformation of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 oligomers and their ATPase activity.
claims.source: Here, we provide evidence that RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 directly interact with a subset of factors involved in the initiation of the NMD response and these interactions can affect greatly the conformation of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 oligomers and their ATPase activity.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: DHX34 is an RNA helicase that binds SMG1 and UPF1 and promotes the interaction of UPF1 with UPF2 and UPF3b, UPF1 phosphorylation and the initiation of NMD.
claims.source: DHX34 is an RNA helicase that binds SMG1 and UPF1 and promotes the interaction of UPF1 with UPF2 and UPF3b, UPF1 phosphorylation and the initiation of NMD (Hug and Cáceres, 2014; Melero et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies cited.

claims.claim: Variants of DHX34 unable to facilitate UPF1 phosphorylation have been found as pathogenic versions specific to inherited forms of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS).
claims.source: Interestingly, variants of DHX34 unable to facilitate UPF1 phosphorylation have been found as pathogenic versions specific to inherited forms of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) (Rio-Machin et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on a recent study cited.

claims.claim: The N-termini of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 contain two histidine residues, His25 and His27 in RUVBL2, that bind the nucleotide and contribute to maintain it within its binding pocket.
claims.source: The N-termini of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 contain two histidine residues, His25 and His27 in RUVBL2, that bind the nucleotide and contribute to maintain it within its binding pocket (Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019; Silva et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous structural studies cited.

claims.claim: DHX34 directly affects the conformation of RUVBL2 N-termini and decreases ATP hydrolysis.
claims.source: Here, cryo-EM reveals that the NMD factor DHX34 directly affects the conformation of RUVBL2 N-termini and decreases ATP hydrolysis.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on cryo-EM and biochemical data.

claims.claim: DHX34 distorts the N-terminal regions in all three RUVBL2 subunits that are not visible in the map, an indication that they are flexible and not attached to the hexameric ring after DHX34 binding.
claims.source: DHX34 distorts the N-terminal regions in all three RUVBL2 subunits that are not visible in the map, an indication that they are flexible and not attached to the hexameric ring after DHX34 binding.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM data.

claims.claim: These changes provide an exit route for nucleotides, which are lost in all the RUVBL2 subunits.
claims.source: Thus, these changes provide an exit route for nucleotides, which are lost in all the RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural and biochemical data.

claims.claim: DHX34 down-regulates the ATPase activity of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex in vitro.
claims.source: We find that DHX34 down-regulates the ATPase activity of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on ATPase activity measurements.

claims.claim: These effects are mediated exclusively by changes in RUVBL2 and not in RUVBL1, as shown by RUVBL2 ATPase-dead mutants not being sensible to DHX34.
claims.source: Importantly, these effects are mediated exclusively by changes in RUVBL2 and not in RUVBL1, as shown by RUVBL2 ATPase-dead mutants not being sensible to DHX34.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ATPase activity measurements with different mutants.

claims.claim: DHX34 stabilizes a conformation of RUVBL2 unable to hydrolyze ATP.
claims.source: Together, these results show that DHX34 stabilizes a conformation of RUVBL2 unable to hydrolyze ATP.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined structural and biochemical data.

claims.claim: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 do not always share the same function in vivo.
claims.source: Some evidence supports this model. Several reports indicate that RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 do not always share the same function in vivo (Mao and Houry, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on a review cited.

claims.claim: The ATPase activity of RUVBL2 is several fold higher than RUVBL1 at least when expressed separately.
claims.source: The ATPase activity of RUVBL2 is several fold higher than RUVBL1 at least when expressed separately (Nano et al., 2020), suggesting they do not function in the same way.
claims.evidence: This is based on a study cited.

claims.claim: RUVBL2 binds RPAP3 and PIH1D1, two subunits of the R2TP complex, functions not shared by RUVBL1.
claims.source: Along the same lines, RUVBL2 shows several specialized functions in the context of the R2TP complex. RUVBL2 binds RPAP3 and PIH1D1, two subunits of the R2TP complex, functions not shared by RUVBL1.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the R2TP complex.

claims.claim: Cordycepin, a derivative of the nucleoside adenosine affects the circadian clock in mammals by targeting RUVBL2.

results.result: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 are AAA-type ATPases that form hetero-hexameric rings with alternating subunits, containing six nucleotide-binding domains. The hexamer has two distinct faces (ATPase-face and DII-face) defined by protruding domain II (DII) structures, and nucleotides co-purify with the complex even without supplementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 describe well-established structural features of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes supported by multiple prior structural studies and citations. The claims are consistent with Figure 1A and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

results.result: DHX34 directly interacts with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hetero-hexamers both in vitro and in cells. Among tested NMD factors (UPF1, UPF2, UPF3b, EJC, DHX34), only DHX34 formed a stable direct complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C39-C41 are supported by pull-down experiments (Figure 1B) and immunoprecipitation data from cells (Figures 1C-E). The negative results for other NMD factors strengthen the specificity of the DHX34-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 interaction.

results.result: SMG1 forms a direct complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2, but this interaction excludes SMG8 and SMG9, which normally inhibit SMG1 kinase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 are supported by reciprocal pull-down experiments using His-tagged RUVBL1 and FLAG-tagged SMG1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F). The absence of SMG8/SMG9 in the complex is an interesting observation, though the functional implications require further investigation.

results.result: Cryo-EM analysis reveals that DHX34 binds to the DII-face of hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 rings, disrupting dodecameric double-ring complexes. The structure was determined at 5.0 Å average resolution, with differential resolution (4.1 Å for RUVBL1-RUVBL2 core, 8-10 Å for DHX34) indicating flexible attachment of DHX34.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are supported by cryo-EM data including 2D averages (Figure 2B), 3D reconstructions, and resolution analysis (Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2). The resolution disparity is appropriately interpreted as evidence for flexibility, consistent with the extensive classification required.

results.result: DHX34 binding induces loss of N-terminal density in all three RUVBL2 subunits but not in RUVBL1 subunits, coupled with loss of nucleotide from all RUVBL2 subunits while nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 are supported by high-resolution cryo-EM analysis (4.2 Å for the masked RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring) and extensive 3D classification experiments (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 3-5). The differential effects on RUVBL1 vs RUVBL2 are clearly demonstrated and the resolution argument (C60) is valid.

results.result: DHX34 induces conformational changes primarily in the internal DII domains and AAA-ring regions. The RUVBL1 nucleotide-binding pocket remains intact (explaining retained ADP binding), while the RUVBL2 nucleotide-binding pocket structure is preserved but nucleotide is lost due to N-terminal displacement.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C66 are supported by structural comparisons with the crystal structure (PDB 2XSZ) shown in Figure 3 and Video 1. The interpretation that N-terminal displacement causes nucleotide loss (C65) is reasonable given the structural data, though alternative mechanisms cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: The RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex has a 3:3:1 stoichiometry (three RUVBL1, three RUVBL2, one DHX34). Volume analysis indicates ~120 kDa for DHX34 density, consistent with monomeric DHX34 (132 kDa) or core domains (111 kDa), and DHX34 lacking the CTD can still bind RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by volume analysis using EMAN, comparison with isolated DHX34 structure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), and deletion experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). The convergence of multiple lines of evidence (volume, mass calculation, deletion) strongly supports the 3:3:1 stoichiometry.

results.result: Domain mapping reveals that no single domain of DHX34 is necessary and sufficient for RUVBL1-RUVBL2 binding. Multiple domains contribute to the interaction, with heavily truncated versions showing reduced but detectable binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by systematic domain deletion experiments in cells (Figure 4B-D). The quantification shows that all single deletions retain binding, and even large truncations maintain some interaction, consistent with the structural observation of multiple contact points.

results.result: DHX34 reduces RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ATPase activity by ~50%. This effect is mediated exclusively through RUVBL2, as demonstrated by the lack of effect on RUVBL2 ATPase-dead mutants (His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2^E300Q) while RUVBL1 ATPase-dead mutants (His-RUVBL1^E303Q-RUVBL2) remain sensitive to DHX34.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84, C89 are supported by systematic ATPase assays using wild-type and mutant complexes (Figure 5A-C, Figure 5—figure supplements 2-3). The use of single-subunit mutants provides strong evidence for RUVBL2-specific regulation. The experimental design appropriately controls for protein stability and linearity of measurements.

results.result: The His-tag on RUVBL1 does not interfere with DHX34's regulatory effect. Untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2 shows similar ATPase activity and DHX34-mediated inhibition as His-tagged complexes, with the same RUVBL2-specific mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 are supported by parallel experiments with tagged and untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). This control is important for validating that the observed effects are not artifacts of the purification tag.

results.result: There is a direct correlation between DHX34-induced conformational changes in RUVBL2 N-termini and reduced ATP hydrolysis activity. DHX34 stabilizes a conformation of RUVBL2 that is unable to hydrolyze ATP, with effects mediated exclusively through RUVBL2.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C95, C98-C100 integrate structural and biochemical data to establish mechanism. The correlation is well-supported by the combination of cryo-EM showing N-terminal displacement and nucleotide loss (Figure 3) with ATPase assays showing RUVBL2-specific inhibition (Figure 5).

results.result: The ATPase-dead mutant His-RUVBL1^E303Q-RUVBL2^E300Q forms oligomers similar to wild-type and has similar thermal stability. The DHX34^D279A mutant retains 24.2% ATPase activity compared to wild-type DHX34, and DHX34 stability is maintained for 20 min at 37°C but compromised by 40 min.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 describe important controls for the ATPase experiments. The data are supported by negative-stain EM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), thermal stability measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,F), and ATPase assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E). These controls validate the experimental design.

results.result: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 directly interact with NMD initiation factors (DHX34 and SMG1), and these interactions profoundly affect the conformation and ATPase activity of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 oligomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91, C116 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating the interaction data (Figures 1B-E), structural analysis (Figures 2-3), and biochemical characterization (Figure 5). The evidence from multiple complementary approaches strongly supports these conclusions.

results.result: DHX34 may couple RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ATPase activity to the assembly of NMD initiation complexes, with ATP hydrolysis inhibition potentially stabilizing the DHX34-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 interaction while awaiting other NMD factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C114-C115, C117 are speculative interpretations about the functional role in NMD. While the biochemical and structural data are solid, the connection to NMD complex assembly is not directly demonstrated. The model is reasonable but requires validation through additional experiments examining NMD factor recruitment and complex assembly.

results.result: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 may have specialized functions within the hexameric complex. Evidence includes differential ATPase activities when expressed separately, RUVBL2-specific binding to R2TP components (RPAP3, PIH1D1), and RUVBL2-specific targeting by cordycepin.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 synthesize evidence from the literature to support functional specialization. The cited evidence (differential ATPase activity, R2TP interactions, cordycepin binding) is appropriate, and the current study's findings of RUVBL2-specific regulation by DHX34 add to this model. However, C106 is somewhat speculative.

results.result: ATP binding/hydrolysis is essential for RUVBL1-RUVBL2 function in vivo across all studied pathways. The low in vitro ATPase activity suggests the complex functions as a regulated switch rather than a processive motor, with ATP hydrolysis potentially serving to disengage RUVBL1-RUVBL2 from partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 appropriately summarize established knowledge from the literature with proper citations. The interpretation that RUVBL1-RUVBL2 functions as a switch (C108) is reasonable given the low ATPase activity, though it remains somewhat speculative. The model is consistent with the current findings.

results.result: ATP binding/hydrolysis by RUVBL1-RUVBL2 is essential for cellular activities but purified proteins show weak in vitro ATPase activity. Interacting proteins (PIH1D1, Ino80) can induce conformational changes in the ATPase ring, including changes in RUVBL2 N-terminal regions that interact with nucleotide.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C13 summarize prior work with appropriate citations. These establish the context for the current study by showing that (1) ATPase activity is functionally important, (2) activity is low in vitro, and (3) partners can induce conformational changes. This background is accurate and relevant.

results.result: RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ATPase activity is required for multiple cellular pathways including Fanconi Anemia, telomerase assembly, and NMD. In each case, ATPase-dead mutants fail to rescue the phenotypes caused by RUVBL1/RUVBL2 depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17, C31-C32 accurately summarize prior work demonstrating the importance of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ATPase activity across multiple pathways. The citations are appropriate and the claims establish the biological significance of understanding ATPase regulation.

results.result: NMD removes aberrant transcripts with premature termination codons (PTCs) and regulates physiological transcript abundance. NMD initiation involves formation of the SURF complex (UPF1, SMG1, eRF1/3) where SMG1 is inhibited by SMG8/SMG9, followed by remodeling through UPF2/UPF3b/EJC interaction leading to UPF1 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 provide accurate background on NMD mechanism based on established knowledge and appropriate citations. This context is essential for understanding the significance of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 and DHX34 in NMD regulation.

results.result: DHX34 is a DEAH-box RNA helicase required for NMD initiation that promotes UPF1 phosphorylation. DHX34 binds both UPF1 (via RecA domains) and SMG1 (via CTD), and pathogenic variants found in familial AML/MDS reduce UPF1 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C30 accurately summarize prior work on DHX34 with appropriate citations. The connection to AML/MDS (C29-C30) establishes clinical relevance. This background is essential for understanding why DHX34-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 interactions are important to study.

results.result: RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes were purified as equimolar heteromers forming dodecameric double-ring structures. Masking DHX34 and OB-fold domains during image processing improved the resolution of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring to 4.2 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C53 describe methodological approaches that are well-supported by the data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3A, Table 1). The masking strategy is a standard and appropriate approach for improving resolution of the more stable core structure.

results.result: DHX34 binds to internal DII domain regions of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hexamer, leaving external OB-fold domains accessible for other interactions. DHX34 contacts multiple RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 subunits, inducing global conformational changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by the cryo-EM structure (Figure 2C). The observation that OB-folds remain accessible (C51) is reasonable based on the structure, though the speculation about availability for other partners requires experimental validation.

results.result: DHX34 binds SMG1 and UPF1, promotes UPF1-UPF2-UPF3b interactions and UPF1 phosphorylation. Pathogenic DHX34 variants in familial AML/MDS are unable to facilitate UPF1 phosphorylation. RUVBL2 N-termini contain histidines (His25, His27) that bind nucleotide.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 accurately cite prior work establishing DHX34 function and the structural basis for nucleotide binding. These provide essential context for interpreting the current findings about DHX34-mediated regulation of RUVBL2.

results.result: DHX34 distorts RUVBL2 N-terminal regions making them flexible and detached from the hexameric ring, providing an exit route for nucleotides that are lost from all RUVBL2 subunits.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 interpret the structural data (missing density for RUVBL2 N-termini, absence of nucleotide) to propose a mechanism. The interpretation is reasonable and consistent with the data, though the specific mechanism of nucleotide release could involve additional factors not captured in the structure.

results.result: NMD initiation requires assembly of transient macromolecular complexes. SMG1 phosphorylates UPF1 only after proper interactions occur, triggering transition from SURF to DECID complex and mRNA decay. DHX34 promotes these interactions and activates UPF1 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 provide accurate background on NMD mechanism from the literature. This context is important for the Discussion's interpretation of how RUVBL1-RUVBL2 might function in NMD complex assembly.
